title: Writing for Broadcast: How to Sound Like A Real Person (summarising Kern, Sound Reporting)
rule: Write the way you speak; picture one listener; contractions; everyday words ('but' not 'however', 'robbery' not 'heist'); short sentences, subject first, active voice; skip rhetorical questions ('Have you ever wondered...?') because listeners cannot answer; limit names and numbers.
example: 'Teachers and principals have told students to report sexual harassment' over the passive original; 'however' becomes 'but'.
llm_tell: Rhetorical-question openers, formal connectives ('however', 'moreover'), and stat-heavy sentences read aloud are the exact things this guide bans.

title: UBC LFS400 Workshop: Writing For the Ear
rule: One thought per sentence (watch and/but/or as a sign of two thoughts); about three words per second of airtime; a sentence should fit one normal breath; subject-verb-object; round figures; replace measurements with analogies; avoid homonyms, acronyms, tongue twisters; one telling detail, not piled adjectives; 'mouth edit': say the opening from memory, compare with the page, fix what is awkward to say. Echo endings are a gimmick; twists work better in the last third than at the very end.
example: 'Nearly 15000' rounded; 'the size of a football field' instead of a measurement.
llm_tell: Piled adjectives, tidy echo/callback endings and a closing twist or 'so-what' abstraction are the shapes an LLM defaults to; this guide flags echo as a gimmick.

title: Speechwriting in Perspective (CRS Report 98-170)
rule: Write to be heard, not read; punctuate for the ear. Average spoken sentence is 8 to 16 words (written can run to 30). Repetition with variation is a basic tool; rhythmic triads work 'provided the device is not overused'. Use aural signposts (secondly, finally). No more than three major points. Colons and semicolons make compound sentences hard to process.
example: 'The average spoken sentence runs from eight to 16 words.'
llm_tell: Overused triads and uniform cadence; the report itself warns against overuse of the device.

title: Radio Listeners Can't Detect AI Voice, But Trust Issues Remain
rule: Listeners could not tell a synthetic voice from a human one reading the same script: 59% of the human-voice group said human, 55% of the AI-voice group also said human. Only humour differed significantly (33% vs 26% called it funny). Disclosure moved opinion: told it was AI, 20% viewed the clip less favourably vs 4% for human. Trade-press survey, n=1,326, two short ad-type scripts, same script for both reads.
example: Human 59% correct; AI mistaken for human by 55%.
llm_tell: It tests voice only. It says nothing on whether LLM-written script text is detectable; scripts were identical in both arms. Humour is the one gap.

title: speech-draft skill (agensi.io)
topic: AI speech tells and delivery rules
rule: Pace length at about 130 words per minute; sentences under 20 words; add pauses and stage directions; avoid stock openers like 'I'm happy to be here'. Listing page (search snippet) also says it flags delve/tapestry vocabulary, 'not just X, it's Y', em-dash overuse, rule-of-three pile-ups, uniform sentence cadence, generic conclusion openers. Vendor page, no data.
example: 'I'm happy to be here' as the avoided opener.
llm_tell: Uniform cadence; rule-of-three pile-ups; 'not just X, it's Y'; generic opener and closer. Unmeasured, vendor claim.

title: On Speaking Well summary (Peggy Noonan)
rule: Short sentences because the audience hears rather than reads; read drafts aloud and mark what is hard to say; clause-heavy sentences leave the speaker breathless or misplace emphasis; write like a network news writer; no speech over about 20 minutes; humour matters. Secondary summary, not Noonan's own text.

title: New book for political speechwriters (Lehrman, Political Speechwriter's Companion)
rule: Per Lehrman (via blurb/news snippets, not the book): students are taught not to repeat, yet repetition gives spoken words force; anaphora and antimetabole make lines memorable; framework LAWS (language, anecdote, wit, support); the book distinguishes language people understand from language people remember. Book itself not read.
llm_tell: Repetition is a legitimate spoken device, so repeated structure alone is not a tell; stacking it everywhere is.

title: Sonic Format (audio drama script format)
rule: Audio drama has no visuals: sound cues get their own capitalised, numbered line (SFX); scene headings give location and time; setting is built by sound; about one page of dialogue is roughly one minute. Search snippets only. No source found on the 'as you know' exposition problem.

title: Studies of LLM-written speech scripts detected by listeners
rule: Searched twice; found no controlled study of listeners detecting LLM-written script text. Only voice-synthesis detection studies (UCL: 73% detection of synthetic speech; 85% when paired with human clip) were found, via search summary only. BBC Academy, NPR's own writing guide and Noonan's/Lehrman's own text were not reached (503/DNS failure/not surfaced).
